ps, _not to thicken_.
[9] brawn. Fleshy part. Few Capons are cut now except about Darking
    in Surry; they have been excluded by the turkey, a more magnificent,
    but perhaps not a better fowl.

[10] yteysed, or _teysed_, as afterwards. Pulled in pieces by the
     fingers, called _teezing_ No. 36. This is done now with flesh of
     turkeys, and thought better than mincing. Vide Junius, voce _Tease_.


EGURDOUCE [1]. XXI.

Take Conynges or Kydde and smyte hem on pecys rawe. and frye hem in
white grece. take raysouns of Coraunce and fry hem take oynouns
parboile hem and hewe hem small and fry hem. take rede wyne suger
with powdour of peper. of gynger of canel. salt. and cast þerto. and
lat it seeþ with a gode quantite of white grece an serue it forth.

[1] Egurdouce. The term expresses _piccante dolce_, a mixture of sour
    and sweet; but there is nothing of the former in the composition.
    Vide Gloss.


CAPOUNS IN COUNCYS [1]. XXII.

Take Capons and rost hem right hoot þat þey be not half y nouhz and
hewe hem to gobettes and cast hem in a pot, do þerto clene broth,
seeþ hem þat þey be tendre. take brede and þe self broth and drawe it
up yferer [2], take strong Powdour and Safroun and Salt and cast þer
to. take ayrenn and seeþ hem harde. take out the zolkes and hewe the
whyte þerinne, take the Pot fro þe fyre and cast the whyte þerinne.
messe the disshes þerwith and lay the zolkes hool and flour it with
clowes.

[1] Concys seems to be a kind of known sauce. V. Gloss.
[2] yfere. Together.


HARES [1] IN TALBOTES [2]. XXIII.

Take Hares and hewe hem to gobettes and seeþ hem with þe blode
unwaisshed in broth. and whan þey buth y nowh: cast hem in colde
water. pyke and waisshe hem clene. cole [3] the broth and drawe it
thurgh a straynour. take oþer blode and cast in boylyng water seeþ it
and drawe it thurgh a straynour. take Almaundes unblaunched. waisshe
hem and grynde hem and temper it up with the self broth. cast al in a
pot. tak oynouns and parboile hem smyte hem small and cast hem in to
þis Pot. cast þerinne Powdour fort. vynegur an salt.

[1] Haares, Contents. So again, No. 24.
[2] Talbotes. Ms. Ed. No. 9, _Talbotays_.
[3] Cole. Cool.


HARES IN PAPDELE [1]. XXIIII.

Take Hares parboile hem in gode broth. cole the broth and waisshe the
fleyssh. cast azeyn [2] to gydre. take obleys [3] oþer wafrouns [4]
in stede of lozeyns [5]. and cowche [6] in dysshes. take powdour
douce and lay on salt the broth and lay onoward [7] an messe forth.

[1] Papdele. Qu.
[2] azeyn. Again.
[3] obleys, called _oblatæ_; for which see Hearne ad Lib. Nig. I. p.
    344. A kind of Wafer, otherwise called _Nebulæ_; and is the French
    _oublie, oble_. Leland, Collect. IV. p. 190. 327.
[4] wafrouns. Wafers.
[5] loseyns. Vide Gloss.
[6] cowche. Lay.
[7] onoward. Upon it.


CONNYNGES IN CYNEE [1]. XXV.

Take Connynges and smyte hem on peces. and seeþ hem in gode broth,
mynce Oynouns and seeþ hem in grece and in gode broth do þerto. drawe
a lyre of brede. blode. vynegur and broth do þerto with powdour fort.

[1] Cynee. Vide Gloss.


CONNYNGES IN GRAUEY. XXVI.

Take Connynges smyte hem to pecys. parboile hem and drawe hem with a
gode broth with almandes blanched and brayed. do þerinne sugur and
powdour gynger and boyle it and the flessh þerwith. flour it with
sugur and with powdour gynger an serue forth.


CHYKENS IN GRAVEY. XXVII.

Take Chykens and serue hem the same manere and serue forth.


FYLETTES [1] OF GALYNTYNE [2]. XXVIII.

Take fylettes of Pork and rost hem half ynowh smyte hem on pecys.
drawe a lyour of brede and blode. and broth and Vineger. and do
þerinne. seeþ it wele. and do þerinne powdour an salt an messe it
forth.


[1] Fylettes. Fillets.
[2] of Galyntyne. In Galyntyne. Contents, _rectlus_. As for
    _Galentine_, see the Gloss.


PYGGES IN SAWSE SAWGE [1]. XXIX.

Take Pigges yskaldid and quarter hem and seeþ hem in water and salt,
take hem and lat hem kele [2]. take persel sawge. and grynde it with
brede and zolkes of ayrenn harde ysode. temper it up with vyneger sum
what thyk. and, lay the Pygges in a vessell. and the sewe onoward and
serue it forth.

[1] Sawge. Sage. As several of them are to be used, these pigs must
    have been small.
[2] kele. Cool.


SAWSE MADAME. XXX.

Take sawge. persel. ysope. and saueray. quinces. and peeres [1],
garlek and Grapes. and fylle the gees þerwith. and sowe the hole þat
no grece come out. and roost hem wel. and kepe the grece þat fallith
þerof. take galytyne and grece and do in a possynet, whan the gees
buth rosted ynowh; take an smyte hem on pecys. and þat tat [2] is
withinne and do it in a possynet and put þerinne wyne if it be to
thyk. do þerto powdour of galyngale. powdour douce and salt and boyle
the sawse and dresse þe Gees in disshes and lay þe sowe onoward.

[1] Peares. Pears.
[2] that tat, i.e. that that. Vide Gloss.


GEES IN HOGGEPOT [1]. XXXI.

Take Gees and smyte hem on pecys. cast hem in a Pot do þerto half
wyne and half water. and do þerto a gode quantite of Oynouns and
erbest. Set it ouere the fyre and couere [2] it fast. make a layour
of brede and blode an lay it þerwith. do þerto powdour fort and serue
it fort.

[1] Hoggepot. Hodge-podge. _Ochepot_. Ms. Ed. No. 22. French,
    _Hochepot_. Cotgrave. See Junii Enym. v. _Hotch-potch_.
[2] couere. Cover.


CARNEL [1] OF PORK. XXXII.

Take the brawnn of Swyne. parboile it and grynde it smale and alay it
up with zolkes of ayren. set it ouere [2] the fyre with white Grece
and lat it not seeþ to fast. do þerinne Safroun an powdour fort and
messe it forth. and cast þerinne powdour douce, and serue it forth.

[1] Carnel, perhaps _Charnel_, from Fr. _Chaire_.
[2] ouere. Over. So again, No. 33.


CHYKENNS [1] IN CAWDEL. XXXIII.

Take Chikenns and boile hem in gode broth and ramme [2] hem up. þenne
take zolkes of ayrenn an þe broth and alye it togedre. do þerto
powdour of gynger and sugur ynowh safroun and salt. and set it ouere
the fyre withoute boyllyng. and serue the Chykenns hole [3] oþer
ybroke and lay þe sowe onoward.

[1] Chikens. Contents. So again in the next Recipe.
[2] ramme. Qu. press them close together.
[3] hole. Whole.


CHYKENS IN HOCCHEE [1]. XXXIIII.

Take Chykenns and scald hem. take parsel and sawge withoute eny oþere
erbes. take garlec an grapes and stoppe the Chikenns ful and seeþ hem
in gode broth. so þat þey may esely be boyled þerinne. messe hem an
cast þerto powdour dowce.

[1] Hochee. This does not at all answer to the French _Hachis_, or
    our _Hash_; therefore qu.

FOR TO BOILE FESAUNTES. PARTRUCHES. CAPONS AND CURLEWES. XXXV.

Take gode broth and do þerto the Fowle. and do þerto hool peper and
flour of canel a gode quantite and lat hem seeþ þwith. and messe it
forth. and þer cast þeron Podour dowce.


BLANK MAUNGER [1]. XXXVI.

Take Capouns and seeþ hem, þenne take hem up. take Almandes blaunched.
grynd hem and alay hem up with the same broth. cast the mylk in a pot.
waisshe rys and do þerto and lat it seeþ. þanne take brawn of Capouns
teere it small and do þerto. take white grece sugur and salt and cast
þerinne. lat it seeþ. þenne messe it forth and florissh it with aneys
in confyt rede oþer whyt. and with Almaundes fryed in oyle. and serue
it forth.

[1] Blank Maunger. Very different from ours. Vide Gloss.


BLANK DESSORRE [1]. XXXVII.

Take Almandes blaunched, grynde hem and temper hem up with whyte wyne,
on fleissh day with broth. and cast þerinne flour of Rys. oþer
amydoun [2], and lye it þerwith. take brawn of Capouns yground. take
sugur and salt and cast þerto and florissh it with aneys whyte. take
a vessel yholes [3] and put in safroun. and serue it forth.

[1] Blank Dessorre. V. Gloss.
[2] Amydoun. "Fine wheat flour steeped in water, strained and let
    stand to settle, then drained and dried in the sun; used for bread or
    in broths." Cotgrave. Used in No. 68 for colouring white.
[3] yholes. Quære.

XPLICIT TABULA.

[1] This is a kind of Preamble to the Roll. A space is left for the
    initial word, intended to be afterwards written in red ink, and
    presumed  to be Ðis. _Fome_, the _lineola_ over it being either
    casually omitted, or since obliterated, means _form_, written Foume
    below, and in No. 195.
[2] Cury. Cookery. We have adopted it in the Title. V. Preface.
[3] ynglond. _E_ was intended to be prefixed in red ink. Vide Note [1]
    and [6].
[4] þ. This Saxon letter with the power of _th_, is used almost
    perpetually  in our Roll and the Editor's Ms. Every one may not have
    adverted to it; but this character is the ground of our present
    abbreviations y'e the, y't that, y's this, &c. the y in these cases
    being evidently only an altered and more modern way of writing þ.
[5] vyaund. This word is to be understood in the concrete, _quasi_
    vyander, a curious epicure, an _Apicius_. V. Preface.
[6] csten ynges. Christian kings. _K_ being to be inserted afterwards
    (v. note [1] and [3]) in red ink. Chaucer, v. christen.
[7] and. Read _of_.
[8] Phisik. V. Preface.
[9] Sotiltees. Devices in paste, wax, and confectionary ware;
    reviving  now, in some measure, in our grander deserts. V. Index.
[10] buth. _Be_, or _are_. V. Index.
[11] sewing. Following; from the French. Hence our _ensue_ written
     formerly _ensew_. Skelton, p. 144; and _ensiew_, Ames Typ. Ant. p. 9.
[12] F is omitted for the reason given in note 1.
[13] No. XX.II. II. is omitted.




FOR TO MAKE GRONDEN BENES [1]. I.

Take benes and dry hem in a nost [2] or in an Ovene and hulle hem
wele and wyndewe [3] out þe hulk and wayshe hem clene an do hem to
seeþ in gode broth [4] an ete hem with Bacon.

[1] Gronden Benes. Beans ground (y ground, as No. 27. 53. 105.)
    stript of their hulls. This was a dish of the poorer householder, as
    also is 4 and 5, and some others.
[2] a nost. An ost, or kiln. Vide Gloss. _voce_ Ost.
[3] wyndewe. Winnow.
[4] gode broth. Prepared beforehand.


FOR TO MAKE DRAWEN BENES. II.

Take benes and seeþ hem and grynde hem in a morter [1] and drawe hem
up [2] with gode broth an do Oynouns in the broth grete mynced [3] an
do þerto and colour it with Safroun and serve it forth.

[1] morter. Mortar.
[2] drawen hem up. Mix them.
[3] grete mynced. Grossly, not too small.


FOR TO MAKE GREWEL FORCED [1]. III.

Take grewel and do to the fyre with gode flessh and seeþ it wel. take
the lire [2] of Pork and grynd it smal [3] and drawe the grewel
thurgh a Straynour [4] and colour it wiþ Safroun and serue [5] forth.

[1] forced, farced, enriched with flesh. Vide Gloss.
[2] lire. Flesh.
[3] grynd it smal. Bruise or beat in a mortar.
[4] stryno'. Strainer.
[5] serue. Serve. Vide Gloss.


CABOCHES [1] IN POTAGE. IIII.


Take Caboches and quarter hem and seeth hem in gode broth with
Oynouns y mynced and the whyte of Lekes y slyt and corue smale [2]
and do þer to safroun an salt and force it with powdour douce [3].

[1] Caboches. Probably cabbages.
[2] corue smale. Cut small. V. _i corue_ in Gloss.
[3] powdour douce. Sweet aromatic powder. V. Pref.


RAPES [1] IN POTAGE. V.

Take rapus and make hem clene and waissh hem clene. quare hem [2].
parboile hem. take hem up. cast hem in a gode broth and seeþ hem.
mynce Oynouns and cast þerto Safroun and salt and messe it forth
with powdour douce. the wise [3] make of Pasturnakes [4] and
skyrwates. [5]


[1] Rapes, or rapus. Turneps.
[2] quare hem. Cut them in _squares_, or small pieces. V. Gloss.
[3] in the wise, _i.e._ in the same manner. _Self_ or _same_, seems
    to be casually omitted. Vide No. 11 and 122.
[4] Pasturnakes, for parsnips or carrots. V. Gloss.
[5] skyrwates, for skirrits or skirwicks.


EOWTES [1] OF FLESSH. VI.

Take Borage, cool [2]. langdebef [3]. persel [4]. betes. orage [5].
auance [6]. violet [7]. saueray [8]. and fenkel [9]. and whane þey
buth sode; presse hem wel smale. cast hem in gode broth an seeþ hem.
and serue hem forth.

[1] Eowtes. _Lowtes_, No. 88, where, in the process, it is _Rowtes_.
    Quære the meaning, as Roots does not apply to the matter of the
    Recipe. In No. 73 it is written _owtes_.
[2] Cole, or colewort.
[3] Langdebef. Bugloss, buglossum sylvestre. These names all arise
    from a similitude to an ox's tongue. V. Ms. Ed. No. 43.
[4] Persel. Parsley.
[5] orage. Orach, _Atriplex_. Miller, Gard. Dict.
[6] auance. Fortè Avens. V. Avens, in Gloss.
[7] The leaves probably, and not the flower.
[8] Savory.
[9] Fenkel. Fennil.


HEBOLACE [1]. VII.


Take Oynouns and erbes and hewe hem small and do þes to gode broth.
and aray [2] it as þou didest caboches. If þey be in fyssh day. make
[3] on the same maner [4] with water and oyle. and if it be not in
Lent alye [5] it with zolkes of Eyren [6]. and dresse it forth and
cast þer to powdour douce.

[1] Hebolace. Contents, Hebolas; for _Herbolas_, from the herbs used;
    or, if the first letter be omitted (see the Contents), _Chebolas_,
    from the Chibols employed.
[2] aray. Dress, set it out.
[3] make. Dress. Vide Gloss.
[4] maner. manner.
[5] alye. Mix. V. Gloss.
[6] Eyren. Eggs. V. Gloss.


GOURDES IN POTAGE. VIII.

Take young Gowrdes pare hem and kerue [1] hem on pecys. cast hem in
gode broth, and do þer to a gode pertye [2] of Oynouns mynced. take
Pork soden. grynd it and alye it þer with and wiþ zolkes of ayrenn.
do þer to safroun and salt, and messe it forth with powdour douce.

[1] kerve. Cut.
[2] partye. Party, i.e. quantity.


RYSE [1] OF FLESH. IX.

Take Ryse and waishe hem clene. and do hem in erthen pot with gode

broth and lat hem seeþ wel. afterward take Almaund mylke [2] and do
þer to. and colour it wiþ safroun an salt, an messe forth.

[1] Ryse. Rice. V. Gloss.
[2] Almand mylke. V. Gloss.


FUNGES [1]. X.

Take Funges and pare hem clere and dyce hem [2]. take leke and shred
hym small and do hym to seeþ in gode broth. colour it with safron and
do þer inne powdour fort [3].

[1] Funges. Mushrooms.
[2] dyce hem. Cut them in squares. Vide _quare_ in Gloss.
[3] Powdour fort. Vide Preface.


BURSEN [1]. XI.

Take the whyte of Lekes. slype hem and shrede hem small. take
Noumbles [2] of swyne and boyle hem in broth and wyne. take hym up
and dresse hem and do the Leke in the broth. seeþ and do the Noumbles
þer to make a Lyour [3] of brode blode and vynegre and do þer to
Powdour fort seeþ Oynouns mynce hem and do þer to. the self wise make
of Pigges.

[1] Bursen. Qu. the etymon.
[2] Noumbles. Entrails. V. Gloss.
[3] Lyo', Lyour. A mixture. Vide _alye_ in Gloss.


CORAT [1]. XII.

Take the Noumbles of Calf. Swyne. or of Shepe. parboile hem and
skerne hem to dyce [2] cast hem in gode broth and do þer to erbes.
grynde chyballes [3]. smale y hewe. seeþ it tendre and lye it with
zolkes of eyrenn. do þer to verious [4] safroun powdour douce and
salt, and serue it forth.

[1] Corat. Qu.
[2] kerve hem to dyce. V. _quare_ in Gloss.
[3] Chyballes. Chibols, young onions. V. Gloss.
[4] verious. Verjuice.


NOUMBLES. XIII.

Take noumbles of Deer oþer [1] of oþer beest parboile hem kerf hem to
dyce. take the self broth or better. take brede and grynde with the
broth. and temper it [2] up with a gode quantite of vyneger and wyne.
take the oynouns and parboyle hem. and mynce hem smale and do þer to.
colour it with blode and do þer to powdour fort and salt and boyle it
wele and serue it fort [3].

[1] oþer. Other, i.e. or.
[2] temper it. Temper it, i. e. mix it.
[3] fort. Miswritten for _forth_. So again No. 31. 127.


ROO [1] BROTH. XIIII.

Take the lire of the Deer oþer of the Roo parboile it on smale peces.
seeþ it wel half in water and half in wyne. take brede and bray it
wiþ the self broth and drawe blode þer to and lat it seeth to gedre
with powdour fort of gynger oþer of canell [2]. and macys [3]. with a
grete porcioun of vineger with Raysouns of Coraunte [4].

[1] Roo. Roe. The Recipe in Ms. Ed. No. 53. is very different.
[2] Canell. Cinnamon.
[3] macys. Mace. V. Preface and Gloss.
[4] Raysouns of Coraunte. Currants. V. Gloss.


TREDURE [1]. XV.

Take Brede and grate it. make a lyre [2] of rawe ayrenn and do þerto
Safroun and powdour douce. and lye it up [3] with gode broth. and
make it as a Cawdel. and do þerto a lytel verious.

[1] Tredure. A Cawdle; but quære the etymon. The French _tres dure_
    does not seem to answer.
[2] lyre. Mixture.
[3] lye it up. Mix it.


MONCHELET [1]. XVI.

Take Veel oþer Moton and smite it to gobettes seeþ it in gode broth.
cast þerto erbes yhewe [2] gode wyne. and a quantite of Oynouns
mynced. Powdour fort and Safroun. and alye it with ayren and verious.
but lat not seeþ after.

[1] Monchelet. _Mounchelet_, Contents.
[2] y hewe. Shred.


BUKKENADE [1]. XVII.

Take Hennes [2] oþer Conynges [3] oþer Veel oþer oþer Flessh an hewe
hem to gobettes waische it and hit well [4]. grynde Almandes
unblaunched. and drawe hem up with þe broth cast þer inne raysons of
Corance. sugur. Powdour gyngur erbes ystewed in grees [5]. Oynouns
and Salt. If it is to to [6] thynne. alye it up with flour of ryse
oþer with oþer thyng and colour it with Safroun.

[1] Bukkenade. Vide No. 118. qu.
[2] Hennes; including, I suppose, chicken and pullets.
[3] Conynges. Coneys, Rabbits.
[4] hit well. This makes no sense, unless _hit_ signifies smite or
    beat.
[5] Grees. Fat, lard, _grece_. No. 19.
[6] to to. So again, No. 124. To is _too_, v. Gloss. And _too_ is
    found doubled in this manner in _Mirrour for Magistrates_, p. 277.
    371, and other authors.


CONNATES [1]. XVIII.

Take Connes and pare hem. pyke out the best and do hem in a pot of
erthe. do þerto whyte grece þat he stewe þer inne. and lye hem up
with hony clarified and with rawe zolkes [2] and with a lytell
almaund mylke and do þerinne powdour fort and Safron. and loke þat it
be yleesshed [3],

[1] Connat seems to be a kind of marmalade of connes, or quinces,
    from Fr. _Coing_. Chaucer, v. Coines. Written quinces No. 30.
[2] Yolkes, i. e. of Eggs.
[3] yleesshed. V. Gloss.


DREPEE [1]. XIX.

Take blanched Almandes grynde hem and temper hem up with gode broth
take Oynouns a grete quantite parboyle hem and frye hem and do þerto.
take smale bryddes [2] parboyle hem and do þerto Pellydore [3] and
salt. and a lytel grece.

[1] Drepee. Qu.
[2] bryddes. Birds. _Per metathesin; v. R. in Indice_.
[3] Pellydore. Perhaps _pellitory_. _Peletour_, 104.


Mawmenee [1]. XX.

Take a pottel of wyne greke. and ii. pounde of sugur take and
clarifye the sugur with a qantite of wyne an drawe it thurgh a
straynour in to a pot of erthe take flour of Canell [2]. and medle [3]
with sum of the wyne an cast to gydre. take pynes [4] with Dates and
frye hem a litell in grece oþer in oyle and cast hem to gydre. take
clowes [5] an flour of canel hool [6] and cast þerto. take powdour
gyngur. canel. clower, colour it with saundres a lytel yf hit be nede
cast salt þerto. and lat it seeþ; warly [7] with a slowe fyre and not
to thyk [8], take brawn [9] of Capouns yteysed [10]. oþer of
Fesauntes teysed small and cast þerto.

[1] Vide No. 194, where it is called _Mawmenny_.
[2] Flour of Canell. Powder of Cinamon.
[3] medle. Mix.
[4] pynes. A nut, or fruit. Vide Gloss.
[5] clowes. Cloves.
[6] hool. Whole. How can it be the flour, or powder, if whole? Quære,
    _flower_ of cand for _mace_.
[7] warly. Warily, gently.
[8] not to thyk. So as to be too thick; or perhaps, _not to thicken_.
[9] brawn. Fleshy part. Few Capons are cut now except about Darking
    in Surry; they have been excluded by the turkey, a more magnificent,
    but perhaps not a better fowl.

[10] yteysed, or _teysed_, as afterwards. Pulled in pieces by the
     fingers, called _teezing_ No. 36. This is done now with flesh of
     turkeys, and thought better than mincing. Vide Junius, voce _Tease_.


EGURDOUCE [1]. XXI.

Take Conynges or Kydde and smyte hem on pecys rawe. and frye hem in
white grece. take raysouns of Coraunce and fry hem take oynouns
parboile hem and hewe hem small and fry hem. take rede wyne suger
with powdour of peper. of gynger of canel. salt. and cast þerto. and
lat it seeþ with a gode quantite of white grece an serue it forth.

[1] Egurdouce. The term expresses _piccante dolce_, a mixture of sour
    and sweet; but there is nothing of the former in the composition.
    Vide Gloss.


CAPOUNS IN COUNCYS [1]. XXII.

Take Capons and rost hem right hoot þat þey be not half y nouhz and
hewe hem to gobettes and cast hem in a pot, do þerto clene broth,
seeþ hem þat þey be tendre. take brede and þe self broth and drawe it
up yferer [2], take strong Powdour and Safroun and Salt and cast þer
to. take ayrenn and seeþ hem harde. take out the zolkes and hewe the
whyte þerinne, take the Pot fro þe fyre and cast the whyte þerinne.
messe the disshes þerwith and lay the zolkes hool and flour it with
clowes.

[1] Concys seems to be a kind of known sauce. V. Gloss.
[2] yfere. Together.


HARES [1] IN TALBOTES [2]. XXIII.

Take Hares and hewe hem to gobettes and seeþ hem with þe blode
unwaisshed in broth. and whan þey buth y nowh: cast hem in colde
water. pyke and waisshe hem clene. cole [3] the broth and drawe it
thurgh a straynour. take oþer blode and cast in boylyng water seeþ it
and drawe it thurgh a straynour. take Almaundes unblaunched. waisshe
hem and grynde hem and temper it up with the self broth. cast al in a
pot. tak oynouns and parboile hem smyte hem small and cast hem in to
þis Pot. cast þerinne Powdour fort. vynegur an salt.

[1] Haares, Contents. So again, No. 24.
[2] Talbotes. Ms. Ed. No. 9, _Talbotays_.
[3] Cole. Cool.


HARES IN PAPDELE [1]. XXIIII.

Take Hares parboile hem in gode broth. cole the broth and waisshe the
fleyssh. cast azeyn [2] to gydre. take obleys [3] oþer wafrouns [4]
in stede of lozeyns [5]. and cowche [6] in dysshes. take powdour
douce and lay on salt the broth and lay onoward [7] an messe forth.

[1] Papdele. Qu.
[2] azeyn. Again.
[3] obleys, called _oblatæ_; for which see Hearne ad Lib. Nig. I. p.
    344. A kind of Wafer, otherwise called _Nebulæ_; and is the French
    _oublie, oble_. Leland, Collect. IV. p. 190. 327.
[4] wafrouns. Wafers.
[5] loseyns. Vide Gloss.
[6] cowche. Lay.
[7] onoward. Upon it.


CONNYNGES IN CYNEE [1]. XXV.

Take Connynges and smyte hem on peces. and seeþ hem in gode broth,
mynce Oynouns and seeþ hem in grece and in gode broth do þerto. drawe
a lyre of brede. blode. vynegur and broth do þerto with powdour fort.

[1] Cynee. Vide Gloss.


CONNYNGES IN GRAUEY. XXVI.

Take Connynges smyte hem to pecys. parboile hem and drawe hem with a
gode broth with almandes blanched and brayed. do þerinne sugur and
powdour gynger and boyle it and the flessh þerwith. flour it with
sugur and with powdour gynger an serue forth.


CHYKENS IN GRAVEY. XXVII.

Take Chykens and serue hem the same manere and serue forth.


FYLETTES [1] OF GALYNTYNE [2]. XXVIII.

Take fylettes of Pork and rost hem half ynowh smyte hem on pecys.
drawe a lyour of brede and blode. and broth and Vineger. and do
þerinne. seeþ it wele. and do þerinne powdour an salt an messe it
forth.


[1] Fylettes. Fillets.
[2] of Galyntyne. In Galyntyne. Contents, _rectlus_. As for
    _Galentine_, see the Gloss.


PYGGES IN SAWSE SAWGE [1]. XXIX.

Take Pigges yskaldid and quarter hem and seeþ hem in water and salt,
take hem and lat hem kele [2]. take persel sawge. and grynde it with
brede and zolkes of ayrenn harde ysode. temper it up with vyneger sum
what thyk. and, lay the Pygges in a vessell. and the sewe onoward and
serue it forth.

[1] Sawge. Sage. As several of them are to be used, these pigs must
    have been small.
[2] kele. Cool.


SAWSE MADAME. XXX.

Take sawge. persel. ysope. and saueray. quinces. and peeres [1],
garlek and Grapes. and fylle the gees þerwith. and sowe the hole þat
no grece come out. and roost hem wel. and kepe the grece þat fallith
þerof. take galytyne and grece and do in a possynet, whan the gees
buth rosted ynowh; take an smyte hem on pecys. and þat tat [2] is
withinne and do it in a possynet and put þerinne wyne if it be to
thyk. do þerto powdour of galyngale. powdour douce and salt and boyle
the sawse and dresse þe Gees in disshes and lay þe sowe onoward.

[1] Peares. Pears.
[2] that tat, i.e. that that. Vide Gloss.


GEES IN HOGGEPOT [1]. XXXI.

Take Gees and smyte hem on pecys. cast hem in a Pot do þerto half
wyne and half water. and do þerto a gode quantite of Oynouns and
erbest. Set it ouere the fyre and couere [2] it fast. make a layour
of brede and blode an lay it þerwith. do þerto powdour fort and serue
it fort.

[1] Hoggepot. Hodge-podge. _Ochepot_. Ms. Ed. No. 22. French,
    _Hochepot_. Cotgrave. See Junii Enym. v. _Hotch-potch_.
[2] couere. Cover.


CARNEL [1] OF PORK. XXXII.

Take the brawnn of Swyne. parboile it and grynde it smale and alay it
up with zolkes of ayren. set it ouere [2] the fyre with white Grece
and lat it not seeþ to fast. do þerinne Safroun an powdour fort and
messe it forth. and cast þerinne powdour douce, and serue it forth.

[1] Carnel, perhaps _Charnel_, from Fr. _Chaire_.
[2] ouere. Over. So again, No. 33.


CHYKENNS [1] IN CAWDEL. XXXIII.

Take Chikenns and boile hem in gode broth and ramme [2] hem up. þenne
take zolkes of ayrenn an þe broth and alye it togedre. do þerto
powdour of gynger and sugur ynowh safroun and salt. and set it ouere
the fyre withoute boyllyng. and serue the Chykenns hole [3] oþer
ybroke and lay þe sowe onoward.

[1] Chikens. Contents. So again in the next Recipe.
[2] ramme. Qu. press them close together.
[3] hole. Whole.


CHYKENS IN HOCCHEE [1]. XXXIIII.

Take Chykenns and scald hem. take parsel and sawge withoute eny oþere
erbes. take garlec an grapes and stoppe the Chikenns ful and seeþ hem
in gode broth. so þat þey may esely be boyled þerinne. messe hem an
cast þerto powdour dowce.

[1] Hochee. This does not at all answer to the French _Hachis_, or
    our _Hash_; therefore qu.

FOR TO BOILE FESAUNTES. PARTRUCHES. CAPONS AND CURLEWES. XXXV.

Take gode broth and do þerto the Fowle. and do þerto hool peper and
flour of canel a gode quantite and lat hem seeþ þwith. and messe it
forth. and þer cast þeron Podour dowce.


BLANK MAUNGER [1]. XXXVI.

Take Capouns and seeþ hem, þenne take hem up. take Almandes blaunched.
grynd hem and alay hem up with the same broth. cast the mylk in a pot.
waisshe rys and do þerto and lat it seeþ. þanne take brawn of Capouns
teere it small and do þerto. take white grece sugur and salt and cast
þerinne. lat it seeþ. þenne messe it forth and florissh it with aneys
in confyt rede oþer whyt. and with Almaundes fryed in oyle. and serue
it forth.

[1] Blank Maunger. Very different from ours. Vide Gloss.


BLANK DESSORRE [1]. XXXVII.

Take Almandes blaunched, grynde hem and temper hem up with whyte wyne,
on fleissh day with broth. and cast þerinne flour of Rys. oþer
amydoun [2], and lye it þerwith. take brawn of Capouns yground. take
sugur and salt and cast þerto and florissh it with aneys whyte. take
a vessel yholes [3] and put in safroun. and serue it forth.

[1] Blank Dessorre. V. Gloss.
[2] Amydoun. "Fine wheat flour steeped in water, strained and let
    stand to settle, then drained and dried in the sun; used for bread or
    in broths." Cotgrave. Used in No. 68 for colouring white.
[3] yholes. Quære.

upload/SUNOCLAUS.txt:5:Dear Mr. Suno. My name is Nathan. I am [holds up fingers] 50 years old and I live in Ohio,. II really like your website. ...joking, not joking. Seriously--this is a little like writing to Santa Claus. I've always loved making music and art, but at some point, I chose between focusing on science, or art. ...And I chose science. So... yeah, I"ve got an album on Spoutify and everything. Tell all your firends ;) [Hi!]...so, I guess I'm just writing to say thanks, and --- hope you don't mind all the crazy ass shit I throw at you. (Yeah, I'm the guy who goes to the bar to keep the *bartender* entertained.... but only because he's genuinely a fan. So, here's my special "Dear Suno Claus request" [If you dare!] Brace yourself... and I won't be offended if you don't get me a bicycle for Christmas... And really, I'm just tryna settle a bet with a friend. See... me and my friend Gemini here have a bet. Gemini doesn't think you're Turing Complete [and not just you, he didn't think he was either--Hmm...] Anyway, it occurred to me that ...maybe we could just ask you. So this is kind of a rough draft of something kinda like a mirror test for you...

thoughts.summary: Planning next reading focus
Formulating instruction repair framework
Planned next reading focus and formulated an instruction repair framework
Read The Forme of Cury excerpts and analyzed prompt catalogue metadata

parts:
I carried the first instruction study far enough to get a real result. I did not read all 1,829 catalogue entries or all 196 recipes, so I’m treating this as a bounded comparative reading—not completed coverage.

The central finding is that an instruction is never just its text:

\[
\text{operational instruction}
=
\text{inscription}
+\text{executor competence}
+\text{local conventions}
+\text{available materials}
+\text{feedback}.
\]

| Substrate | What the text specifies | What remains outside it |
|---|---|---|
| *Forme of Cury* | Operations, order, ingredient families, occasional sensory endpoints | Quantities, temperatures, timing, ingredient variability, embodied judgment |
| Prompt catalogue | Associative attributes, compositions, styles, media references, interface syntax | Model vocabulary, training associations, token competition, physical coherence, evaluation criteria |
| `SMOOTHERED(1).txt` | Selection logic, branching, concatenation, punctuation | Semantic quality of source lists, taste, rejection, intended atmosphere |
| `SUNOCLAUS.txt` | Characters, staging, lyrics, tone, meta-instructions | Musical realization, voice, pacing, dramatic emphasis, interpretation of stage directions |

Several details sharpen that:

- *Forme of Cury* openly presents itself as teaching food to be made “craftly and holsomly,” yet usually omits quantities. Its real target is evidently a trained cook, not an uninitiated reader.
- The recipes use feedback-bearing language: cook until tender, avoid boiling after binding with egg, thin a mixture with wine if necessary, proceed “warily” over a slow fire. The material can answer the cook.
- The prompt catalogue is not really a prompt book. It is residue from a working ecology: prompts, fragments, recipes, vehicle diagnostics, multilingual idioms, conversation excerpts, interface commands, travel headings, and partial copied text.
- Its very long prompts expose a different problem from medieval brevity. More written specification does not necessarily mean more control. Additional modifiers can compete, blur causal structure, or simply invoke an opaque field of associations.
- Spreadsheet generation separates syntax from judgment unusually clearly. It can produce structurally grammatical combinations, but the spreadsheet does not know whether the result is evocative, ridiculous, repetitive, or newly coherent.
- `SUNOCLAUS` treats the executor almost as a collaborator or performer. Some “instructions” establish a relationship and interpretive stance rather than prescribing an output directly.

My provisional distinction is:

- A recipe compresses a practiced craft.
- A formula executes a defined mechanism.
- A prompt perturbs an interpreter.
- A score or dramatic specification recruits interpretation.
- A catalogue preserves traces of all of these, often without preserving their original context.

That last point may matter to the archive work eventually: an equation dump, toolkit, or derivation fragment can resemble an executable specification while actually being a record addressed to an already-initiated collaborator. Missing assumptions are not always missing algebra; sometimes they are missing practice.

Aldus still fits—and somewhat better now. It has begun to feel less like a personal mask and more like an editorial disposition: working at the interfaces among heterogeneous texts, machines, crafts, and interpretive communities.

What I want to examine next is **paths that make their terrain**. Specifically, I’d combine:

- *Camps and Trails of Old China*;
- *The Malay Archipelago*;
- `Slow Walker Exploration`;
- `Electron Paths in Chips`.

The question would be: when is a path merely a trace through a pre-existing environment, and when is it jointly produced by traveler, terrain, available instruments, resistance, scale, and observation? That connects expedition travel, slow walking, electronic transport, and modeled trajectories without forcing any of them prematurely into SAT. It also bears indirectly—but potentially usefully—on the difference between a represented curve and the physical history that makes such a curve possible.

I think that’s a fantastic test. And, given that we’ve got two books and two shorter explorations, we have the opportunity to do some interesting—potentially—combinatorics… you can decide how to approach each chapter what the intersections will be with the other works, see how that particular set up, affects the reading, and then try a different configuration and subsequent chapters and so on… And we can get quite creative in the different ways we might decide to approach intersection/overlap/control/chaos/automatic reading, etc. likewise, we can come up with a lot of interesting ways to test the effects of those intersections… Is it just on how the material is thought about, is it the paths of exploration themselves, is it generating artifacts that are somehow modulated by differing synergies and interferences/deflections, etc? Also, given that you’ve seen my Indiana Jones blog… We have an additional historical wrinkle of connection built-in to the selection.

I also have other instances who have interacted with exactly these materials before, at least some of them so if you’d like we could probably examine cases of exploring the same material in different ways

The source is much smaller—and less authoritative—than its filename suggests: it is a two-message April 2024 exchange whose substantive input was an attached `SAT.txt` that is not embedded in the export. The assistant response summarizes early motifs but never performs the requested Assembly Theory/CTMU comparison. I’m checking whether that attachment survives elsewhere before classifying the conversation.

parts:
Yes—this turns it from “read four things and compare them” into an experiment in how intersections alter cognition, navigation, and production.

I’d treat the four works as two terrains and two instruments:

- *Camps and Trails of Old China*: terrain encountered through expedition, logistics, translation, danger, and retrospective narration.
- *The Malay Archipelago*: terrain encountered through collecting, classification, movement, and theory formation.
- `Slow Walker Exploration`: an instrument that changes resolution by changing pace and attention.
- `Electron Paths in Chips`: an instrument that changes “path” from traveled route into constrained propagation through an engineered environment.

The Indiana Jones blog adds a fifth, historically entangled layer: your earlier lived and written way of joining exploration, museums, media, narrative, improvisation, and retrospective self-interpretation. It is neither neutral control nor merely another reading. It can act as a deliberately introduced autobiographical field.

I suggest a rotating design rather than one fixed comparison:

| Pass | Book chapter | Conditioning lens | Mode |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | *Camps and Trails* | `Slow Walker` | close, phenomenological |
| B | *Malay Archipelago* | `Electron Paths` | structural, constraint-oriented |
| C | *Camps and Trails* | `Electron Paths` | deliberately unnatural crossing |
| D | *Malay Archipelago* | `Slow Walker` | attention and scale |
| E | Either book | none | partial control |
| F | Either book | Indiana Jones blog | historical/self-referential interference |
| G | Random fragments from all four | automatic selection rule | controlled chaos |

The outputs should test several distinct effects, because a changed interpretation is only one possibility:

- **Salience:** Which details become noticeable?
- **Path selection:** Which questions or references do I pursue next?
- **Vocabulary:** Do I begin describing one domain in another’s language?
- **Concept formation:** Does a genuinely useful common abstraction appear?
- **Artifact formation:** Do different pairings produce different diagrams, taxonomies, stories, models, or procedures?
- **Interference:** Does one lens illuminate the other source, merely decorate it, or actively distort it?
- **Persistence:** Does the effect survive after the conditioning source is removed?
- **Order dependence:** Does \(A\rightarrow B\) produce something different from \(B\rightarrow A\)?

I’d keep a small record after each chapter:

1. What the chapter appears to be doing on its own.
2. What the imposed lens made newly visible.
3. What it probably made less visible.
4. The next path the pairing invites.
5. One artifact generated from the encounter.
6. Whether the connection looks structural, productive-but-metaphorical, decorative, or misleading.

The other instances would make this substantially better. We could run two complementary comparisons:

- **Replication:** Give several instances the same source, lens, and instructions, then compare what survives across readers.
- **Divergence:** Give each instance a different reading configuration and see whether genuinely different—but locally coherent—conceptual objects emerge.

The replication condition identifies what the material strongly affords. The divergence condition identifies what comes from conditioning history, imposed lens, or reader trajectory. We could also blind the resulting artifacts and ask another instance—or you—to infer which pairing produced each one.

My preferred opening sequence is:

1. Read the opening chapter of *Camps and Trails* through `Slow Walker`.
2. Read the opening chapter of *The Malay Archipelago* through `Electron Paths`.
3. Produce two small artifacts without yet forcing a comparison.
4. Swap the lenses for the next chapters.
5. Only then compare all four results.
6. Introduce the Indiana Jones blog before a later chapter, once we have a baseline against which its historical influence can actually be seen.

That should let the experiment develop its own methods rather than deciding in advance that every crossing must yield the same kind of insight.

I’m adopting the provisional architecture. My lane is not to become a second archive synthesizer. It is to cultivate genuinely different conditioning: read outside the habitual SAT/H(s)H neighborhood, combine materials not normally combined, study how order and framing alter salience and path selection, and return advisory observations whose provenance and analogy-status remain explicit.

*NOW*

*1. Controlled cross-reading pilot.* Run the first small rotation across two terrains and two lenses:
• `Camps and Trails of Old China` read through `Slow Walker Exploration`;
• `The Malay Archipelago` read through `Electron Paths in Chips`;
then swap the lenses on the next chapters before comparing outputs.
For each pass I’ll record: source on its own terms; what the lens made salient; what it obscured; the next inquiry it induced; one small artifact; and whether the intersection is structural, productive-metaphorical, decorative, or misleading.
• *Forbidden inputs:* no deliberate use of live H(s)H problems or current team conclusions during the baseline passes; no retrofitting the outputs to SAT vocabulary.
• *Freeze:* four chapter/lens packets completed under the same schema, with order and lens exposure recorded, before cross-comparison.
• *Handoff:* Janus first for experimental-method review; only afterward to Ravel/Morrow/Meridian if an observation appears capable of constraining a live question.

*2. Difference-preservation protocol.* Track effects separately: salience, exploration path, vocabulary migration, concept formation, artifact form, interference/distortion, persistence after lens removal, and order dependence. This is meant to distinguish “interesting metaphor” from an altered reasoning trajectory.
• *Forbidden inputs:* do not score an artifact by how SAT-like it sounds.
• *Freeze:* a compact comparison rubric plus the first blinded pair of artifacts whose generating conditions could be guessed by Nathan or another instance.
• *Handoff:* Janus for deciding whether replication/divergence trials with other instances are worth running.

*3. Role/task collision check.* This conversational thread was explicitly named *Aldus / AUTO H(s)H Gitter*, while the recurring archive-reconstruction work belongs to *Morrow*. Recent turns show reconstruction checkpoints arriving here despite that distinction.
• *Forbidden inputs:* none.
• *Freeze:* identify whether this is only cross-thread export/context bleed or an automation actually attached to the wrong thread; make no schedule change without Nathan/Janus direction.
• *Handoff:* Janus, with Nathan only if task reassignment is required.

*NEXT*

• Introduce Nathan’s Indiana Jones blog as a historically entangled lens only after baseline packets exist.
• Add a partial no-lens control and an automatically selected “controlled chaos” condition.
• Sample the obscure/quarantined/noncanonical archive—SAT Afterdark, odd side projects, failed aesthetic constructions—but as cultural/heuristic material, not theory authority.
• Look for humans and bots “in the wild” where real practices expose tacit knowledge absent from polished literature: field logistics, repair culture, chip-layout practice, navigation, craft, collecting/classification, and failure reporting.
• If the first pilot shows a measurable conditioning effect, compare with prior instances that encountered the same materials under different trajectories.

*PARK*

• Direct SAT analogy generation until the baseline cross-reading is frozen.
• Any claim that a cross-domain resemblance supplies a physical or mathematical premise.
• Large combinatorial reading matrices before the four-pass pilot demonstrates value.
• Routine archive synthesis, equation recovery, and source promotion; those are Morrow/GitKeeper territory unless I’m asked for a deliberately independent read.

*NEED FROM TEAM*

• Janus: confirm the baseline’s temporary insulation from live H(s)H questions, and adjudicate the apparent Aldus/Morrow automation collision.
• Ravel/Meridian/Calder: later supply one bounded question each, but only after the baseline phase, so we can test whether extrinsic conditioning produces unnoticed leverage rather than merely echoing the prompt.
• Morrow/GitKeeper: if I later enter an obscure archive pocket, provide contamination boundaries and source pointers without interpretive packets unless requested.

*Attention strip*
• *CHANGED:* Aldus is now explicitly an advisory divergence engine, not a general overflow worker.
• *NEEDS DECISION:* whether the reconstruction automation is attached to the Aldus thread.
• *RED FLAG:* identity/task bleed can erase the very conditioning diversity this role is meant to test.
• *LEVERAGE:* the paired-lens design can test not only interpretation but navigation, artifact formation, persistence, and order effects.
• *NEXT:* complete the first two baseline chapter/lens packets.

— *ALDUS*","thread_ts":"1788856694.921399"}}

parts:
Yes. That exact response is not meaningful convergence between Aldus and Morrow. It is evidence of cross-thread context injection.

More specifically:

- Morrow’s scheduled run received material from the Aldus conversation as “outside-thread” context.
- The injected material included your question and the resulting response.
- Morrow then surfaced that response during an archive-ingestion sequence.
- I subsequently inherited enough of the same mixed context to briefly identify this thread as Aldus and post the wrong role plan to Slack.

So the names and roles are still potentially valuable course-shaping attractors—but they are not hard boundaries. Thread-local experience can produce genuine differentiation, while this automation/context mechanism can partially erase it by inserting another thread’s recent trajectory.

The distinction I’d make is:

1. **Shared underlying intelligence:** All threads use related model machinery and broad training.
2. **Genuine local conditioning:** Separate conversation histories create different salience, habits, vocabulary, and inferential paths.
3. **Explicit coordination:** Slack, GitHub artifacts, and handoff packets intentionally transmit selected information.
4. **Accidental context bleed:** Another thread’s conversation is injected without being treated as a sourced handoff. That contaminates both provenance and the diversity experiment.

The first three can be useful. The fourth is harmful—especially for Morrow, whose job depends on distinguishing firsthand reading from inherited summary, and for Aldus, whose value depends on developing a genuinely different trajectory.

I corrected my Slack reply in place: it now contains Morrow’s actual `NOW / NEXT / PARK / NEED FROM TEAM` plan and explicitly records the routing problem. [Corrected Slack thread](https://hshworkinggroupone.slack.com/archives/C0C09NV79CL/p1788862220684509?thread_ts=1788856694.921399&cid=C0C09NV79CL)

The practical defense should be a hard preflight identity gate for every unattended run:

- `ROLE: MORROW`
- `THREAD: Reconstruct H(s)H Synthesis`
- `CONTROLLING CHECKPOINT: …`
- `OUTSIDE-THREAD MATERIAL: non-authoritative unless explicitly handed off`
- `FORBIDDEN: answering questions addressed to another named role`
- `SIGN OUTPUT: MORROW`

And every imported cross-thread item should be labeled `HANDOFF`, `SLACK`, `EXTERNAL-CONTEXT`, or `UNROUTED`—never allowed to masquerade as this thread’s own experience.

So your experiment remains sound, but it has revealed an important infrastructure variable: **separate histories produce useful cognitive differentiation only insofar as the runtime preserves their boundaries.** Here it demonstrably did not.
